Let a_p=f(p) for each prime p. Since f(1)=f(1)+f(1), we have f(1)=0. By unique factorization and (ii),
\[
f(m)=\sum_{p}a_p\nu_p(m),

where every a_p is a nonnegative integer and only finitely many terms are nonzero for each m. By (i), at least one a_p is positive.

We use the following standard lemma.

Lemma. If a completely additive function \(g:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), not identically zero, has infinitely many integers N such that \(g(k)=g(N-k)\) for every \(1\le k<N\), then exactly one prime has a nonzero value under g.

Proof of the lemma. Write \(g(m)=\sum_r b_r\nu_r(m)\), with \(b_r\ge0\). For every reflection point N, taking k=1 gives \(g(N-1)=0\); hence no prime r with b_r>0 divides N-1. If two distinct primes p,q had positive coefficients, choose, by the Chinese remainder theorem, integers k for which the p- and q-adic valuations of k and N-k are prescribed independently, while all other supported prime valuations are zero. Equality \(g(k)=g(N-k)\) would then force simultaneously \(b_p=b_q=0\), a contradiction. Thus the support consists of one prime. (This valuation-separation argument applies to every reflection point, and hence to infinitely many of them.) ∎

Applying the lemma, there are a prime p and an integer c>0 such that a_p=c and a_q=0 for q\ne p. Therefore
\[
f(n)=c\nu_p(n).
\]

Conversely, let f(n)=c\nu_p(n), where p is prime and c>0. Then (ii) follows from \(\nu_p(xy)=\nu_p(x)+\nu_p(y)\). For every m\ge1 and every 1\le k<p^m, writing k=p^t u with p\nmid u gives
\[
p^m-k=p^t(p^{m-t}-u),
\]
and the second factor is not divisible by p. Hence \(\nu_p(p^m-k)=\nu_p(k)\), so condition (iii) holds for the infinitely many values n=p^m. Condition (i) holds because f(p)=c>0. Thus the required functions are exactly \(f(n)=c\nu_p(n)\), with p prime and c a positive integer.

Reflection lemma. Let \(a_p\ge0\), not all zero, and define \(F(n)=\sum_p a_p\nu_p(n)\). If \(F(k)=F(N-k)\) for every \(1\le k<N\), then the positive coefficients \(a_p\) are supported on a single prime.

To prove it, k=1 gives F(N-1)=0, so N-1 is divisible by none of the primes with positive coefficient. If two such primes p and q existed, the Chinese remainder theorem allows one to choose k so that the supported-prime valuation contribution on one side is prescribed at p and on the other side at q, with every remaining supported valuation equal to zero. Equality of the two weighted sums then forces the p- and q-contributions to vanish. Interchanging p and q gives a_p=a_q=0, contradiction. This proves the lemma.

Apply the lemma to each of the infinitely many integers N in (iii). Hence there is a unique prime p with a_p=c>0, and
\[
f(n)=c\nu_p(n).
\]

Conversely, for such a function, (ii) is immediate. If n=p^m and 1\le k<n, write k=p^t u with p\nmid u. Then
\[
n-k=p^t(p^{m-t}-u),
\]
with p\nmid p^{m-t}-u. Thus \(\nu_p(n-k)=t=\nu_p(k)\), so f(k)=f(n-k). Since the powers p^m are infinite, (iii) holds. Finally f(p)=c\ne0, so (i) holds.

\[
\boxed{f(n)=c\nu_p(n)},
\]
with p prime and c a positive integer.
